# The Worn Key

Ines had tuned pianos for twenty-two years, and she could usually tell the story of a house by the instrument in it. The ones in rich homes were glossy and dead, played twice a year at parties, their hammers still fuzzy as new tennis balls. The ones in churches were exhausted and loyal. The ones in apartments above bars had cigarette burns on the fallboard and a C-sharp that had been pounded flat by someone who only knew three songs, all of them sad.

The piano in Walter Brandt's front room was an old Baldwin upright, walnut, the veneer lifting at one corner like the page of a book someone had fallen asleep reading. Walter had called her himself. He was eighty-one, he said on the phone, and he wanted it tuned properly. Not for selling. Just properly.

He met her at the door in a cardigan buttoned wrong by one hole, so that the whole thing sat slightly askew on him, and she liked him immediately for it.

"It hasn't been done in a while," he said. "Four years. Maybe five."

"That's all right. They forgive you."

"Do they?"

"Mostly."

He led her in and then retreated to the kitchen, the way the good clients did, leaving her alone with the work. She opened the lid, removed the front panel, and ran a quick chromatic scale to hear what she was dealing with.

That was when she noticed the key.

It was the D above middle C. The ivory on it was worn nearly through, a shallow dip in the center like the step of an old stone staircase, the kind you find in cathedrals where eight hundred years of feet have hollowed the rock. Around it, the other keys were yellowed but whole. Only the D had been touched so many times that it had begun to disappear.

Ines had seen wear patterns before. Children practicing the same scale. A composer who favored one key signature. But never a single note, alone, worn like that. Not a chord. Not a phrase. One note.

She played it. It was badly out, sagging almost a quarter-tone flat, the strings tired from being struck more than their neighbors. She tuned the rest of the piano first, working outward from A the way she'd been taught, her lever turning the pins in small, careful increments, listening for the beats between the strings to slow and slow and vanish. It took nearly two hours. The house was quiet except for the refrigerator and, occasionally, the sound of Walter turning a page in the kitchen.

When she came back to the D, she paused.

"Mr. Brandt?"

He appeared in the doorway.

"This key," she said. "The ivory's nearly gone. I can replace it, if you want. I have some good replacement tops in the van. It would match fairly well."

He came and stood beside her and looked down at it for a long time.

"No," he said. "Leave it, please."

She waited. She had learned that people will tell you things if you give them enough silence to put the words in.

"My wife played," he said finally. "Ruth. Not well. She'd tell you that herself. She learned as a girl and gave it up and took it back up when our son went to college, because the house was too quiet. She could do some Chopin, badly. A few hymns." He smiled. "She played 'Moon River' at every party whether anyone asked or not."

"Everyone should have a song like that."

"That D," he said, and touched it without pressing it. "That started as a joke. This house is bigger than it looks, and I'm half deaf, and I was always out in the garage or down in the basement. She didn't like to shout. So one day she just played that note. One note. And I came up to see what she wanted. And after that, it was how she called me."

"Just the one note?"

"The one note. For dinner. For the phone. For come look at this bird. For the car's making that noise again." He laughed quietly. "Forty years of that note. I'd hear it through two floors and a closed door. I could hear it over the lawnmower. I don't know how."

Ines looked at the key again, at the soft hollow in the center of it.

"The last three years," Walter said, "she had a stroke. She couldn't talk much after that. Words came out wrong, or didn't come out at all. It frustrated her terribly. She was a talker, Ruth. But she could still get to the piano. She could still play that one note." He was quiet a moment. "So she used it for everything. For I need help. For I'm fine. For where are you. For nothing, sometimes. Just to know I'd come."

"And you came."

"Every time."

The refrigerator hummed. Outside, a car went past slowly, its radio briefly audible and then gone.

"She died in March," he said. "Two years ago. I haven't touched the piano since. But I keep hearing it. Isn't that stupid. I'll be down in the basement and I'll hear that D and I'll be halfway up the stairs before I remember."

"It's not stupid," Ines said.

He nodded, not quite believing her, and went back to the kitchen.

She tuned the D last. She took her time with it, bringing it up out of its long sag, listening to the three strings of the unison until they stopped arguing and settled into one clear voice. She tuned it better than she had tuned anything in years. When she was done, she replaced the panels, closed the lid over the strings, and sat for a moment with her hands in her lap.

Then, because she could not help it, she pressed the worn key. Once. Gently.

The note went out through the house, round and true.

From the kitchen, she heard a chair scrape back. Footsteps, quick at first, then slowing in the hallway. Then stopping.

After a long time, Walter appeared in the doorway. His face was wet, and he was not trying to hide it.

"I'm sorry," Ines said. "I shouldn't have."

"No," he said. He came over and stood beside the piano and laid his hand on the lid, flat, the way you'd lay a hand on the shoulder of someone you loved. "No. It sounds right now. It sounds the way it's supposed to."

He paid her in cash, and gave her too much, and would not take any back. At the door, she noticed his cardigan was still buttoned wrong, and she almost said something, and then didn't.

Driving home, she kept her radio off. She thought about the stone steps in old cathedrals. She thought about how the things we love are worn down by our love for them, and how that wearing is not damage.

It is only proof that someone kept coming back.
